title: I wanted to see how quickly AI could help me make a commercial game. ~15 human hours later, Photon Fighters is live.
author: ShreddedCheddar32
selftext:
I decided to run a little experiment: could AI dramatically reduce the time and technical barrier required for one person to make a small, genuinely enjoyable commercial game?

I deliberately kept the scope small and started building Photon Fighters, a twin-stick arcade shooter.

Claude and ChatGPT handled essentially all of the code. My role was design, direction, testing, identifying problems, balancing mechanics, and deciding what needed to change.

What surprised me most was how much depth emerged from relatively simple systems interacting.

The finished game has 50 encounters, 10 Guardian bosses, vulnerability windows, near misses, combos, score multipliers, and perfect-encounter streaks. Aggressive, risky play is rewarded, but mistakes can be costly.

I've managed a 4,058,769-point no-death run, and I'm convinced there's a much higher score ceiling.

My estimated human time investment:

\- \~10 hours developing and playtesting

\- \~5 hours creating the trailer and preparing the storefront

\- \~15 hours total to commercial release

The game launched yesterday on itch.io for $2.99.

The development portion of the experiment was fascinating. AI dramatically compressed implementation time, but design decisions, testing, and judging whether something actually felt fun were still essential.

Now comes the second half: finding out whether anyone will actually pay for it.

I'm curious whether others using AI for game development have experienced a similar shift toward spending more time designing/testing than implementing.
